summary: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node. It grows and shrinks dynamically, and inserting or deleting at a known position needs no shifting.

sections.heading: Node structure
sections.body: A list is identified by a `head` pointer to the first node; the last node's `next` is NULL.
sections.code:
struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; };
struct Node *head = NULL;   // empty list

sections.heading: Traversal
sections.code:
for (struct Node *p = head; p; p = p->next)
  printf("%d ", p->data);

sections.heading: Insertion
bullets: At head: new->next = head; head = new. O(1).
At tail: walk to the last node (O(n)), or keep a tail pointer (O(1)).
After a node p: new->next = p->next; p->next = new. O(1) once p is known.

sections.heading: Deletion
sections.body: To delete a node you need the node before it. Deleting the head just moves `head`. Always free the removed node.

sections.heading: Complexity vs array
bullets: Extra memory: one pointer per node, plus malloc overhead.
Poor cache locality: nodes are scattered in memory.

sections.body: Walk the list keeping `prev`, `cur`, `next`; point each node back at prev. O(n) time, O(1) space.
Move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle. If the list has a cycle, fast eventually meets slow (Floyd's algorithm).

bullets: Doubly linked: prev and next pointers allow O(1) deletion given the node and backward traversal; used by the Linux kernel's `list_head`.
Circular: the last node points to the head; natural for round-robin.

sections.body: Arrays win on indexing, iteration speed, and memory use. Lists win only when you hold node pointers and insert/delete in the middle often, or need stable addresses. In practice arrays are usually faster even for middle insertions on small data.

takeaways: Nodes hold data and a next pointer; `head` identifies the list.
O(1) insert/delete at the head, O(n) search and index access.
Deleting needs the predecessor; use a pointer-to-pointer for clean code.
Master reversal and fast/slow pointer patterns.
